### 12.4 Shutdown protocol
- V1 A run ends when its time is up, when someone stops it, or when the model itself says so.
- V2 Whatever the cause, the same work has to happen.
- V3 The loop has to stop on a boundary (a published consistency point).
- V4 The task each device (any attached participant in the periphery) runs on has to be woken out of whatever it was blocked on.
- V5 Every resource acquired for the run has to be released before `run!` returns.
- V6 This section specifies that sequence, which it calls the tail throughout.
- V7 It also specifies the two things that bracket the tail.
- V8 One is the pre-spawn initialization at the top of a run, which is a step of this same protocol.
- V9 The other is the operator interrupt (Ctrl-C in an interactive session), which enters the tail rather than bypassing it.

#### The tail: the ordered sequence every stop takes
- V10 Steps (1) through (5) below run in that order on every stop, whatever initiated it (D-030). [D-030] (bold)
- V11 Steps (6) and (7) specify what happens when a device task or the loop itself ends first.
- V12 Initiation.
- V13 Three events start a shutdown.
- V14 Either `t_end` is reached, or a control-plane stop is issued, or a stop request the advance honours reads `STOP_REQUESTED` in the just-published snapshot (the immutable per-boundary publication) (D-316). [D-316]
- V15 A stop request is an output port of the framework enum `StopFlag`.
- V16 The control-plane stop's issuers are a front end (D-310), a device handle, code, or an operator interrupt (Ctrl-C, treated below). [D-310]
- V17 The third event is model-detected termination (§13.5). [§13.5]
- V18 The loop never stops mid-boundary.
- V19 It always completes the boundary sequence in progress, which a `t` stop places inside a frame (one iteration of the loop).
- V20 It then publishes the final snapshot.
- V21 Only then does it set the sticky stopped status.
- V22 Wake all framework waits.
- V23 The waits are the next-snapshot wait (`wait_next_snapshot(handle)`) and the pause.
- V24 Each waiter observes the stopped status and unwinds.
- V25 A stop issued while paused therefore works.
- V26 Unblock device-specific blocking calls.
- V27 The hook is `unblock!(device)`, default no-op.
- V28 A network input's override closes its own socket, which raises in the blocked task.
- V29 The framework wrapper catches that raise and treats it as shutdown.
- V30 This demotes FlightCore's EOT convention from essential shutdown mechanism to an optional wire-protocol courtesy between remote peers.
- V31 Loop bodies exit.
- V32 The exit is the author's own `while running(handle)` loop, the authoring contract of §11.6. [§11.6]
- V33 That authoring contract teaches two obligations, the predicate check and interruptible blocking (D-373). [D-373]
- V34 Steps (2) and (3) are the framework's half.
- V35 They wake its own waits and call each device's `unblock!`.
- V36 The wrapper's `finally shutdown!(device)` is guaranteed on every exit path.
- V37 Join under the `join_timeout` cap.
- V38 The cap lives on `Control`, the tail's own owner (§12.1, D-256). [§12.1, D-256]
- V39 It is a keyword of the `Simulation` constructor, a positive real in seconds of wall clock, defaulting to 5 (Appendix B). [Appendix B]
- V40 The constructor refuses any other value as `ArgumentInvalid`.
- V41 A device task exceeding the cap is reported by name in a `DeviceJoinTimeout` diagnostic (Appendix C). [Appendix C]
- V42 It is then abandoned rather than left to hang `run!`.
- V43 The diagnostic is written to the loop's own diagnostic cell (each writer's bounded ring of diagnostics and its heartbeat) (D-203). [D-203] (bold)
- V44 The run's-end sweep collects it into the termination record (the stopped-sim value naming how the run ended).
- V45 The logging backend presents it, with the terminal snapshot preceding the join (D-201, D-203). [D-201, D-203]
- V46 Device-initiated paths.
- V47 A device exits voluntarily when its loop body returns, at a window ✕ or a peer EOT.
- V48 No `should_close` hook exists (§11.6). [§11.6]
- V49 With `should_abort` set, the wrapper's exit path also requests a sim stop.
- V50 Otherwise the sim continues with the device's task absent.
- V51 Its staging cell (where the device's pending write batch waits between drains) stops filling, and the loop is structurally indifferent.
- V52 Its roster entry and its claims persist to run end, because §11.3 freezes the roster for the run and death is not detach. [§11.3]
- V53 The roster is the list of attached device entries, and a claim is the set of faces a device may write.
- V54 The orphaned root inputs (the root component's own input faces) hold their last-drained values, visibly (§11.7). [§11.7]
- V55 A crashing device task is caught by the framework wrapper and follows the same path, logged with the device's name (`DeviceCrash`, Appendix C). [Appendix C]
- V56 Loop-side failure.
- V57 A failure on the loop's own side runs steps (1) through (5) from the catch path (D-030). [D-030]
- V58 §13.6 specifies that path, which discards the failed boundary and promotes the previous snapshot to final. [§13.6]
- V59 FlightCore's `SimulationTermination` catch path was the precedent.
- V60 The exception-based termination idiom itself has no place here (§13.5, D-060). [§13.5, D-060]
- V61 Devices therefore unwind cleanly regardless of who died.
- V62 The ordered part, in one line:
- V63 > (1) stop observed → current boundary completed → final snapshot published > → sticky `stopped` set → (2) framework waits woken → (3) `unblock!` > per device → (4) loop bodies return, each through its wrapper's > `finally shutdown!` → (5) join under the `join_timeout` cap → `run!` > returns
- V64 `t_end` lands on the grid.
- V65 The run ends at the first grid boundary whose time reaches or exceeds `t_end` (D-133). [D-133] (bold)
- V66 The run takes whole frames only, never a shortened final step, which grid integrity forbids (§10.4). [§10.4]
- V67 Each grid time is indexed, `tₖ = t₀ + k·h`, and never accumulated.
- V68 The final boundary may therefore overshoot `t_end` by up to `h`.
- V69 The termination record carries the actual final `t` (§13.5). [§13.5]
- V70 This is the `t_plus` spelling (§12.6) applied to the run's own clock. [§12.6]
- V71 The run takes whole frames until the boundary time first covers the duration.
- V72 The two termination sources differ in nature.
- V73 `t_end` is a grid fact, checked against boundary times on the grid.
- V74 Stop requests are checked at every published boundary, `t` included (§13.5). [§13.5]
- V75 The final snapshot goes out before the status is set.
- V76 Publishing first guarantees that output devices can flush the true final state.
- V77 The status in that terminal snapshot carries the run's cumulative diagnostic counters (§11.8), the warning account of a run nobody watched, complete up to that snapshot's own frame top. [§11.8]
- V78 What the tail itself produces comes later by construction.
- V79 It is folded into the termination record and presented through the logging backend, never published (D-201, D-203). [D-201, D-203] (bold)
- V80 That terminal snapshot is retained in the log (the retained sequence of published snapshots) unconditionally, under any `log_every` and any `log_max` (§11.2, D-368). [§11.2, D-368]
- V81 The default of five seconds is generous for front-end window teardown and socket closes.
- V82 It is short enough that an abandoned join reads as a diagnosed timeout rather than a hang.
- V83 The cap is a per-simulation setting, not an implementation constant (D-198). [D-198] (bold)
- V84 That is the disposition §10.4 gives its own two constants, extended here to an operational one (D-198). [§10.4, D-198]
- V85 Deployment contexts legitimately differ in patience.
- V86 An unattended sweep wants to fail fast, a test battery exercising the abandonment path faster still, while a device with slow teardown may warrant more.
- V87 The cap is not trajectory-determining, because the trajectory has ended at the final snapshot before any join begins.
- V88 So replay (the ordinary loop with the drain reading the trace) neither records nor compares the cap (§11.5, §12.7), just as for `log_max` (§11.2). [§11.5, §12.7, §11.2]
- V89 The cap therefore lives on `Control`, not on the `Deployment` (D-256). [D-256]

#### What survives the tail
- V90 After (5) the task set is empty, since device tasks are per-run artifacts (§11.1, D-093). [§11.1, D-093]
- V91 `shutdown!` has also released each device's OS resources.
- V92 What survives a stop is the roster entry, with its binding, claims and stable device id (§11.3). [§11.3]
- V93 A task never survives, and neither does a live resource.
- V94 That holds for a device whose task died mid-run too.
- V95 Its roster entry is indistinguishable at this point from any other's.
- V96 Once stopped, `detach!` can remove a roster entry and release its claims (D-106). [D-106]
- V97 The next run re-acquires everything.
- V98 The next `run!` re-runs device `init!`, since resource acquisition is per-run (D-093). [D-093]
- V99 The precedent is FlightCore's network device, `network.jl`, which created a new socket at each `init!`.
- V100 The next `run!` also spawns fresh tasks against the §12.3 counter, which is never re-armed. [§12.3]
- V101 Each task reads its `last_seen` off the counter at spawn.
- V102 While stopped there are no device tasks at all, so voluntary exit and the §12.2 liveness heartbeat are run-scoped observables. [§12.2]
- V103 A device unplugged while stopped surfaces as the next run's `init!` failure, disposed of by the initialization bracket below.

#### Initialization: the pre-spawn bracket
- V104 Initialization is a step of this protocol, taken at the top of a run (D-138). [D-138] (bold)
- V105 Before any task is spawned, the loop calls `init!` once per roster entry, in attachment order, on the calling task (the task that invoked `run!`).
- V106 Each call sits in its own bracket.
- V107 [code block] for entry in roster                       # attachment order, calling task
- V108 The bracket is what makes "guaranteed on every exit path" (§11.6) true of the path outside that wrapper. [§11.6]
- V109 A device that throws half-way through acquisition is handed back to `shutdown!` right there, so its partially acquired OS resources are released rather than leaked (D-138). [D-138]
- V110 That is exactly why `shutdown!` owes tolerance of a partially initialized device, a rule §11.6 teaches. [§11.6]
- V111 The roster entry is listed for release before its `init!` begins (D-268). [D-268]
- V112 The bracket unlists it once its own `shutdown!` has returned.
- V113 An operator interrupt that escapes the bracket therefore finds listed every device whose `init!` began and that the bracket has not released, and the run releases each before it ends.
- V114 A device listed and not yet initialized can be released having opened nothing, which `shutdown!` tolerates (§11.6). [§11.6]
- V115 The report is the ordinary `DeviceCrash`, not a kind of its own (D-138, Appendix C). [D-138, Appendix C] (bold)
- V116 Its payload (the structured data a diagnostic carries beside its kind) already carries the cause exception and whether `should_abort` was set.
- V117 The diagnostic cell it is written to names the device.
- V118 That is everything an init-time failure has to say.
- V119 The name is honest.
- V120 A device that cannot acquire its resources has crashed before it lived.
- V121 The report is written through the ordinary `report!(address, diagnostic)` entry point, addressed by the roster entry rather than by a handle (D-189). [D-189] (bold)
- V122 There is no device task to hold a handle before the spawn.
- V123 The address supplies the device identity either way, which is why no call passes a device id (§11.8). [§11.8]
- V124 No task is spawned for a failed device, so it is dead from the run's first frame top (D-138). [D-138]
- V125 That needs no machinery.
- V126 Its `task_state` reads `:done` from the first publication (§12.2). [§12.2]
- V127 A device that never ran never beat, so its diagnostic cell also reads stale against the §12.2 threshold from the start (D-138). [§12.2, D-138]
- V128 The claims of a failed device persist to run end (D-138). [D-138]
- V129 This is the death-is-not-detach disposition (§11.3), applied one step earlier than (6)'s. [§11.3]
- V130 The roster is frozen for the run, and the orphaned root inputs hold the values the run started with.
- V131 Those values are well-defined by root-input totality (every root input must hold a value) (§14.6). [§14.6]
- V132 An orphan of (6) holds a last drained batch instead.
- V133 The run's disposition splits on `should_abort`, uniformly with (6) (D-138). [D-138] (bold)
- V134 With the flag clear, which is the default (§11.6), the remaining roster entries initialize, the run starts, and the sim runs with that device absent from the run's first frame. [§11.6]
- V135 That is (6)'s "the sim continues with the device's task absent", shifted to the run's start.
- V136 With the flag set, the failure requests a control-plane stop, and that stop is simply already pending at the run's first frame top.
- V137 This protocol already has that path.
- V138 The loop reads that stop at the frame top, before any frame, so the run advances no frame.
- V139 No new exit protocol is needed, therefore.
- V140 The remaining roster entries still initialize, every rostered device getting its `init!`/`shutdown!` pair uniformly.
- V141 The run ends `stopped` where it started, through this same tail, with its termination record naming the device (§13.5). [§13.5]
- V142 What the operator is left with is an ordinary stopped simulation, a terminal snapshot with the failure named in its diagnostic account.
- V143 It is fully serviceable by §14 and resumable by the next `run!` (§12.6) once the device is plugged back in. [§14, §12.6]
- V144 An `InterruptException` inside a device's `init!` is the operator's stop, not that device's crash (D-268). [D-268] (bold)
- V145 The bracket releases the device through `shutdown!` as for any throw and spawns no task for it.
- V146 In place of the `DeviceCrash` report it sets the `:interrupt` stop through the stop word (the control plane's stop request, one atomic word holding its issuer).
- V147 The run's `should_abort` split above therefore does not arise.
- V148 The remaining roster entries still initialize, and the run ends at its first frame top with zero frames advanced, through the pending-stop path above.
- V149 The device wrapper makes the same discrimination for a raise inside a loop body (§11.6). [§11.6]

#### The operator interrupt
- V150 The operator interrupt is a stop, not a failure (D-132). [D-132] (bold)
- V151 Ctrl-C in an interactive session is a control-plane stop command issued by hand.
- V152 The run completes the current boundary, publishes the final snapshot, takes this tail like any other stop, and ends `stopped`.
- V153 The result is boundary-consistent.
- V154 It is fully serviceable by the §14 stopped-sim services and resumable by the next `run!` (§12.6). [§14, §12.6]
- V155 The interrupt is the escape from a run nothing else ends, and the deviceless run has no other.
- V156 A run with no finite `t_end` and no honoured stop request is the configuration `UnboundedRun` names (Appendix C). [Appendix C]
- V157 The interrupt needs no entry point of its own (D-132). [D-132]
- V158 The stop already rides on the control plane, the separate atomic surface carrying pause, pace and stop (§12.1). [§12.1]
- V159 The exceptions-are-abnormal doctrine (§13.5, D-060) is untouched. [§13.5, D-060]
- V160 That doctrine is about model code, while this is the one exception whose meaning the framework knows.
- V161 The interrupt's scope is the interactive session.
- V162 Outside the REPL, Julia's default (`exit_on_sigint(true)`) kills the process on SIGINT before any of this machinery runs.
- V163 The framework flips nothing process-global (D-132). [D-132]
- V164 Unattended runs, those with empty staging and no snapshot readers, rely on `t_end` and stop requests, as they already must.
- V165 Masking across the boundary is normative, not an implementation hint (D-132). [D-132] (bold)
- V166 The reason is that an `InterruptException` is delivered asynchronously.
- V167 An interrupt landing in the middle of a sweep (one pass through the execution order) would therefore destroy the boundary this protocol is built on completing.
- V168 It would also leave half-written stores (the framework-owned homes of a component's state) (§13.6). [§13.6]
- V169 That forces a choice between `stopped` with dirty stores and a terminal `errored`.
- V170 The `stopped`-with-consistent-stores guarantee is exactly what the masking buys.
- V171 The loop masks delivery across the boundary macro-sequence, using Julia's `disable_sigint`, a sigatomic counter increment that is negligible per frame.
- V172 It takes the deferred raise at the unmask points.
- V173 They are the frame top, where it already consults the control plane (§12.1), and points inside its wait and pause blocks. [§12.1]
- V174 All of those points are boundary-consistent.
- V175 Caught at one of them, the interrupt sets the control-plane stop and enters this tail.
- V176 The catch site (§13.4) therefore never sees a single interrupt. [§13.4]
- V177 A deferred interrupt yields to the frame's own stop request (D-268). [D-268] (bold)
- V178 Stop requests are consulted at each publication and the stop word at the next frame top (§13.5), and the deferred raise lands between the two. [§13.5]
- V179 Where the frame's publication found an honoured request holding, that request is the recorded source and the interrupt is satisfied by the run ending.
- V180 Where none held, the interrupt sets the stop word and the source is `ControlRequestedStop(:interrupt)`.
- V181 A frame that throws with an interrupt pending ends `errored` (D-268). [D-268] (bold)
- V182 The frame's own throw is the disposition (§13.4). [§13.4]
- V183 The catch wraps the cause under the mask and consumes the pending interrupt on its way out.
- V184 The run then takes the abnormal entry under that `StepError` (§13.6). [§13.6]
- V185 The alternative, `stopped` over a half-written boundary, is what the masking exists to prevent.
- V186 The interrupt is satisfied by the run ending.
- V187 An interrupt after a frame's throw does not displace it (D-268). [D-268] (bold)
- V188 `run!`, `replay!` and `step!` store the loop's throw before an interrupt can displace it, and the masked bookkeeping below builds the record from that store.
- V189 The run therefore ends `errored` under its `StepError` wherever a later interrupt lands.
- V190 An interrupt that cuts the handling of the throw itself propagates out of the call raw, and the disposition of the failure is skipped (§13.4). [§13.4]
- V191 The record is still written and the lifecycle is still `errored`.
- V192 The tail's bookkeeping is masked too (D-268). [D-268] (bold)
- V193 After the joins, the run's-end sweep, the termination record and the terminal lifecycle state are written under the same mask.
- V194 An interrupt landing there would otherwise abort the sequence half-way and leave the lifecycle `running`, every service refusing.
- V195 A raise deferred to the end of that bookkeeping propagates out of `run!` raw, the simulation already terminal.
- V196 A forced throw reaches the defensive arm (D-268). [D-268] (bold)
- V197 Julia stops deferring after repeated SIGINTs in a short window, warns that it is forcing the throw, and raises inside the mask.
- V198 That is the one way the branch §13.4 keeps is reached. [§13.4]
- V199 The arm abandons the frame unpublished and the run ends `stopped`, the source `ControlRequestedStop(:interrupt)`.
- V200 The published record is consistent, since the frame published nothing.
- V201 The stores may hold mid-boundary values until the next `init!`, `restore!` or `replay!` resets them.
- V202 The same holds after a throw inside boundary zero (the initialization boundary, the ordinary macro-sequence with an empty integrate) (§13.4). [§13.4]
- V203 `checkpoint` refuses such a run as `CheckpointMidFrame`, since the executor (the compiled form of the stage execution order) no longer rests where its last snapshot was published (§12.6). [§12.6]
- V204 The trace (the primary record of a session) is the reproduction (§12.7). [§12.7]
- V205 A second interrupt during the tail collapses the remaining joins immediately (D-132). [D-132] (bold)
- V206 That is (5)'s abandonment path taken at once, with devices still reported by name (`DeviceJoinTimeout`).
- V207 The run still ends `stopped`.
- V208 Escalation shortens the tail, never reclassifies the run.
